title: Application Security
description: The security every developer handles daily: dependencies, queries, data exposure, validation and secrets.
resumo: 3PP = third-party component; CVE = a known public flaw; CVSS = severity from 0 to 10.
Most CVEs come from transitive dependencies — they ship with your JAR. `mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=...` shows who brings them.
Fix: upgrade the parent or BOM first; otherwise override the version. Run the tests and cite the CVE in the PR.
Scanners in CI (Dependency-Check, Dependabot, Trivy) on every PR and on a schedule.
SQL always parameterized; responses as DTOs; logs without personal data; generic errors to the client.
Validate every input on the server, with allowlists.
A committed secret is a leaked secret: rotate it first, clean the history after.

subsections.subtitle: CVE, CVSS and Third-Party Dependencies (3PP)
subsections.formerSubtitle: CVE, CVSS e Dependências de Terceiros (3PP)
subsections.description: The basic vocabulary of vulnerabilities in libraries.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** your application ships with about a hundred libraries you did not write. When a flaw in one of them becomes public — like Log4Shell — attackers start scanning for it within hours.

**Concept:** 3PP (third-party product) is any component you did not write: Maven libraries, container base images, tools. A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is the public id of a known flaw, in the form CVE-year-number, listed in databases such as the NVD. CVSS scores severity from 0 to 10: low (0.1–3.9), medium (4.0–6.9), high (7.0–8.9) and critical (9.0–10.0). Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) in Log4j 2 scored 10.

**How it works:** the score alone does not decide: what also matters is whether your application uses the vulnerable part, and whether the flaw is being exploited in the wild.
examples.code:
Example scanner alert:

Dependency:  com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:2.13.0
CVE:         CVE-2022-42003
CVSS:        7.5 (High)
Fixed in:    2.13.4.1
Path:        my-api -> spring-boot-starter-web -> spring-boot-starter-json -> jackson-databind

Questions to answer:
1. Which version fixes it?
2. Is the dependency direct or transitive?
3. Does the upgrade break anything (major, minor or patch)?
examples.interview_question: What is a CVE, and how does CVSS help prioritize a fix?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Ignoring an alert because the library is "only transitive". It is inside the JAR you deploy, and reachable through your endpoints just like your own code. Triage it like any other dependency.
examples.code:
WRONG: "jackson-databind is not in our pom.xml, so it is not our problem"
       -> it is in the JAR, and every JSON request goes through it

RIGHT: transitive dependencies ship with the application — triage and fix them

subsections.subtitle: Transitive Dependencies and mvn dependency:tree
subsections.description: Finding out where a vulnerable library comes from.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the scanner reports a CVE in a library that does not appear anywhere in your `pom.xml`.

**Concept:** a direct dependency is one declared in your `pom.xml`. A transitive one comes with another: `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Jackson, Tomcat and many more. Most CVEs are in transitive dependencies. When two paths ask for different versions of the same library, Maven picks the one closest to the root of the tree ("nearest wins") — which explains why an old version can stay in the build.

**How it works:** `mvn dependency:tree` shows who brings each library, and `-Dincludes` filters the tree to the path you care about.
examples.code:
# Full tree
mvn dependency:tree

# Only the path to one library
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind

# Output
[INFO] com.shop:my-api:jar:1.0.0
[INFO] \- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:jar:3.3.4:compile
[INFO]    \- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-json:jar:3.3.4:compile
[INFO]       \- com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:jar:2.17.2:compile

# Newer versions available for the project's dependencies
mvn versions:display-dependency-updates
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between a direct and a transitive dependency, and how do you find out where a library comes from?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Removing a vulnerable library with an `<exclusion>` without checking who needs it. The build passes, but the code that uses it fails at runtime with `NoClassDefFoundError`. Upgrade it instead, and run the tests.
examples.code:
<!-- WRONG: the library disappears, but something still uses it -->
<exclusion>
  <groupId>org.yaml</groupId>
  <artifactId>snakeyaml</artifactId>
</exclusion>
<!-- at startup: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: org/yaml/snakeyaml/LoaderOptions -->

<!-- RIGHT: keep it, at a fixed version (see "Fixing a Vulnerable Dependency") -->

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you know which library is vulnerable and which version fixes it. Now you need to upgrade it without breaking anything.

**Concept:** the best fix is upgrading whatever brings the library — for example the Spring Boot version — because it tested its versions together. When that is not possible, force the fixed version: in Spring Boot projects, override the version property (such as `jackson-bom.version`) or declare the library in `dependencyManagement`. Prefer patch upgrades (2.17.1 → 2.17.2), which only fix bugs; minor and major upgrades can change behavior.

**How it works:** afterwards, confirm the new version with `dependency:tree`, run all the tests, and say in the pull request which CVE it fixes.
examples.code:
<!-- Option 1: upgrade the parent (preferred) -->
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.3.5</version>
</parent>

<!-- Option 2: override the property used by Spring Boot's BOM -->
<properties>
  <jackson-bom.version>2.17.3</jackson-bom.version>
</properties>

<!-- Option 3: pin a transitive dependency -->
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.yaml</groupId>
      <artifactId>snakeyaml</artifactId>
      <version>2.2</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
examples.interview_question: A scanner reported a CVE in a transitive dependency. Which steps do you follow to fix it?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Jumping a major version to fix a CVE without reading the release notes. The CVE is gone, but an API changed and the application fails at runtime. Look for a patch release first; if only a major version fixes it, plan it as its own task.
examples.code:
WRONG: snakeyaml 1.33 -> 2.2 "to fix the CVE", merged after a green build
       -> production: NoSuchMethodError in the YAML config loader

RIGHT: read the release notes / migration guide, run every test level,
       and check the libraries that use it support the new major

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** nobody can track CVEs for a hundred libraries by hand.

**Concept:** scanners compare the project's libraries with CVE databases. OWASP Dependency-Check runs as a Maven plugin and can fail the build above a CVSS score. Dependabot (GitHub) and Renovate open pull requests with the fixed version. Trivy scans container images, including operating-system packages.

**How it works:** scanning every pull request stops a vulnerable version from coming in, and a scheduled scan catches new CVEs in code that did not change.
examples.code:
<!-- pom.xml: fail the build at CVSS 7 or higher -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
  <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
  <version>12.1.0</version>
  <configuration>
    <failBuildOnCVSS>7</failBuildOnCVSS>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

# Run
mvn org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check

# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: maven
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
examples.interview_question: How do you make sure the project does not use libraries with known vulnerabilities?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Scanning only when code changes. A CVE published today affects the version you released last month, and nobody pushes to that repository. Add a scheduled run.
examples.code:
# WRONG: scans only on push and PR
on: [push, pull_request]

# RIGHT: also on a schedule
on:
  push:
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * 1'     # every Monday, even if nobody pushed

subsections.subtitle: SQL Injection
subsections.description: Never build queries from user input.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a search by name builds the SQL by concatenating what the user typed. With `' OR '1'='1`, the query returns every customer.

**Concept:** SQL injection happens when user input becomes part of the SQL command. The defense is to keep the command and the data apart: `PreparedStatement` with `?`, named parameters in JPA (`:name`), or Spring Data derived methods, which are already parameterized.

**How it works:** watch native queries and dynamic `ORDER BY`: a column name cannot be a parameter, so check it against a list of allowed values.
examples.interview_question: What is SQL injection, and how do you prevent it with JDBC and Spring Data JPA?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Concatenating a `LIKE` search into the query to add the `%` wildcards. The wildcards belong in the parameter value, not in the SQL text.

subsections.subtitle: Sensitive Data Exposure
subsections.description: Data that should never leave the application.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** data leaks rarely come from a sophisticated attack. Usually the API returns too much, a log records too much, or an error message shows too much.

**Concept:** the common cases: the API returns the whole entity, with fields like the password hash or a tax id; logs record the full request object; error messages show stack traces, table names or SQL. The defenses: respond with DTOs containing only what is needed, mask personal data in logs, and return generic errors to the client while the details stay in the internal log.

**How it works:** check every new field in a response DTO and every new log line in code review.
examples.interview_question: Name common ways an API exposes sensitive data by accident, and how to avoid them.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Logging a record or object that holds a password. A record's `toString()` prints every component, so the password ends up in the logs. Log only the fields you need, or override `toString`.

subsections.subtitle: Input Validation
subsections.description: All external input is suspect until validated.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the API trusts what arrives. A negative quantity, a 10 MB name or an age of 300 goes straight to the database or breaks a rule.

**Concept:** validating input reduces security flaws and bugs at the same time. With Bean Validation, the rules live in the DTO and Spring rejects the request with 400 before it reaches the service. Validate size, format and range, and prefer allowlists (what is accepted) to denylists (what is blocked).

**How it works:** validation in the frontend is only a convenience: the API must validate again, because anyone can call it directly.
examples.interview_question: Why must the API validate data even if the frontend already does?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A denylist: rejecting input that contains "dangerous" words. Attackers find variations faster than you add them, and real users get blocked. Define what is valid and reject everything else.

subsections.subtitle: Secrets Out of the Code
subsections.description: Passwords and tokens never go into the repository.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a database password in `application.properties` is visible to everyone with access to the repository — and stays in its history forever.

**Concept:** database passwords, API keys and tokens live in environment variables, Kubernetes Secrets or a vault such as HashiCorp Vault — never in code or in a versioned properties file. Tools like gitleaks and GitHub secret scanning find secrets before or after a push.

**How it works:** the properties file only references the variable, and each environment provides the value.
examples.code:
# application.properties: only the reference
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

# Running locally
export DB_PASSWORD='local-password'
./mvnw spring-boot:run

# Search the repository for secrets
gitleaks detect --source .
examples.interview_question: You notice a password was committed. What do you do?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Deleting the secret in a new commit and considering it solved. It is still in the history, and every clone and fork already has it. A committed secret is a leaked secret: rotate it first, then clean the history if needed.
examples.code:
git commit -m "add db config"                 # password inside
git rm config.yml && git commit -m "remove secret"
# still visible: git log -p shows it; clones and forks already have it

# RIGHT
# 1. rotate the password now (the old one is compromised)
# 2. then, if required, rewrite the history (git filter-repo)
